blocks.text: Every four years, millions of Nigerians queue at polling units with their Permanent Voter's Card, waiting to choose a President, 109 senators and 360 members of the House of Representatives. The queue is the visible part. Behind it sit three quieter ideas: who is allowed to vote, how the country is carved into constituencies, and which counting rule turns those votes into seats.

blocks.title: Election, suffrage and constituency
blocks.text: An ELECTION is a formal process by which a defined body of people choose office-holders by voting. SUFFRAGE (or franchise) is the legal right to vote. A CONSTITUENCY is the geographical area whose registered voters elect a representative. Nigeria operates universal adult suffrage: every citizen of 18 years and above who is registered may vote.

blocks.markdown: The 1999 Constitution sets the franchise for each office. Sections 117, 132, 77 and 178 require a voter to be a Nigerian citizen, to have attained the age of **eighteen**, and to be registered on the voters' register of the relevant constituency. An **electoral system** is the set of rules that translates votes into seats or into a declared winner. The three systems examiners ask for are simple majority, the second ballot, and proportional representation.

rows: The candidate with the most votes wins, even if that is less than half

blocks.caption: Three electoral systems. Simple majority is also called plurality or first-past-the-post (FPTP)

blocks.markdown:
### Nigeria's mix of rules

Legislative elections use **first-past-the-post** in single-member constituencies: 109 senatorial districts (three per state plus one for the FCT) and 360 federal constituencies drawn by population.

The **presidential** election is stricter. Under **section 134**, a candidate is elected only if he or she has the highest number of votes **and** not less than one-quarter of the votes in each of at least two-thirds of all the states and the FCT. If that double test is failed, a second election is held between the leading candidate and the runner-up with geographical spread — a form of **second ballot**. Do not write that Nigeria uses only simple majority for every office; the presidency is a qualified-majority system with a run-off.

items: **Conduct of elections** — organise, undertake and supervise elections to the offices of President, Vice-President, Governor, Deputy Governor and members of the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly.
**Voter registration** — compile, maintain and update the national register of voters, and issue voters' cards.
**Party registration and monitoring** — register political parties that meet constitutional conditions, and monitor their organisation, finances and campaigns.
**Constituency delimitation** — divide the country into senatorial districts and federal constituencies.
**Voter and civic education** — inform citizens about the electoral process.
**Referendum** — conduct any referendum required by the Constitution or an Act of the National Assembly.
**Declaration of results** — collate and announce results, and issue certificates of return.

blocks.title: Electoral malpractice
blocks.text: Malpractice is any illegal or dishonest act that distorts the free choice of the electorate. Common Nigerian forms examiners list: ballot-box stuffing and rigging of figures; snatching of ballot boxes; underage voting; vote buying (including the 'see and buy' of photographed ballots); impersonation and multiple voting; inflating accredited numbers; violence and intimidation at polling units; and partisan conduct by electoral officials. Each of these attacks a different part of a free election: who may vote, whether the vote is secret, and whether the count is honest.

blocks.title: Classifying the system used for two Nigerian offices
blocks.prompt: A constituency in Kano returns one member of the House of Representatives. In the same general election a presidential candidate wins the most votes nationwide but fails to obtain 25 per cent in two-thirds of the states. Identify the electoral system applied in each case and state what happens next in the presidential contest.

steps.text: House of Representatives: one member, one constituency, the highest vote wins. That is simple majority / first-past-the-post. There is no requirement to reach 50 per cent, and no second round.
Presidency: section 134 adds a territorial-spread test to the majority of votes. The candidate has failed that test, so he or she is not yet elected.

The Constitution then requires a second election — a run-off — between the candidate with the highest votes and the candidate who has a majority of votes in the highest number of states. That is the second-ballot (run-off) rule.
Name what is not being used. No seats are being shared by party-list percentages, so proportional representation is not in play.
State the examiner's point: Nigeria uses FPTP for the legislature and a qualified majority with possible second ballot for the President. Mixing the two is a common error.

blocks.answer: The House seat is filled by simple majority (FPTP). The presidential candidate is not yet elected; a second-ballot run-off is required under section 134 because the spread test was failed. Proportional representation is not used

blocks.title: INEC, not NEC — and know the malpractice list
blocks.text: The current body is the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), established by the 1999 Constitution (and originally by Decree No. 17 of 1998). FEDECO served the Second Republic; NEC served the aborted Third. Using the wrong initials for the Fourth Republic loses an easy mark. When asked for malpractices, give named forms — rigging, snatching, underage voting, vote buying — not the vague word 'corruption'.

points: An election is the formal choice of office-holders by vote; suffrage is the right to vote; a constituency is the area that elects a representative.
Nigeria uses universal adult suffrage at 18 for registered citizens.

Simple majority (FPTP) awards the seat to the candidate with the most votes; the second ballot requires a further round if a threshold is missed; proportional representation shares seats by vote share.
Nigerian legislative elections use FPTP; the presidential election uses a majority-plus-spread test, with a run-off if the test is failed.
INEC registers parties and voters, delimits constituencies, conducts elections, educates voters and declares results.
Electoral malpractices include rigging, ballot-box snatching, underage voting, vote buying, impersonation, violence and partisan officiating.
